results.summary: This design implements a two-channel XOR stream cipher using programmable Galois LFSRs that can be configured for 32, 16, 8, or 4-bit operation. It provides separate transmit and receive channels, each with enable pins, to encrypt plaintext and decrypt ciphertext bitstreams. A 130-bit serial shift register allows dynamic loading of the LFSR configuration at runtime, with read-back capability for verification. The design includes debug outputs and heartbeat signals, and is intended for educational or experimental cryptographic applications.

Tiny Whisper is a mixed-signal chip that implements a transmitter for the WSPR (Weak Signal Propagation Reporter) protocol in the 3-30 MHz shortwave band. It integrates a digital core containing a CORDIC, a delta-sigma modulator, and local oscillator generation, along with an analog IQ modulator. The design requires external hardware such as an SPI master, UART-to-USB breakout board, and an RF power amplifier with filters and antenna for testing. Documentation is currently incomplete, with references to an external GitHub repository for details.

This project implements a Moore finite state machine for a vending machine controller, handling coin insertion, product selection, and change dispensing. It uses a small datapath for credit tracking and selection, with debounced inputs for coin and buttons. Outputs include dispense and change signals, along with a 4-bit product number, intended to drive LEDs. The design is a simple educational example of an FSM with spaced pulse outputs.

This design is a 10-bit PWM generator with a configuration demultiplexer and double-buffering mechanism. It uses three shadow registers for set, clear, and reload values, which are written via a shared bus and committed simultaneously to update the PWM output. The PWM frequency and duty cycle are determined by the reload, set, and clear values, allowing flexible waveform generation. The design includes reset gating and is intended for applications requiring precise PWM control.

Tiny Calculator is a calculator chip with built-in I/O drivers, implemented in SystemVerilog. It provides arithmetic operations (addition, subtraction, multiplication, division) and supports input from buttons and output to a display via serial and control signals. The pin names indicate connections for a keypad and a seven-segment or LCD display. Documentation is minimal, so the exact usage and external hardware requirements are not fully described.

This project implements a Knight Rider-style LED chaser with PWM brightness control, where the speed and pause functionality are adjustable via three debounced buttons. It drives an 8-LED bargraph or individual LEDs, with outputs cycling in a chasing pattern. The design includes debouncing for the pause, faster, and slower buttons, and operates from a 50 kHz clock. External hardware includes push buttons, a reset button, and a bargraph or 8 LEDs.

This project implements three current-switching DACs for generating analog VGA display signals, using a 16x16 matrix of unit current sources to convert 8-bit digital inputs to analog current sinks. It includes a digital controller that generates VGA control signals and test patterns, and supports both digital RGB222 output via the TinyVGA PMOD and analog outputs requiring external pull-up resistors and opamp circuits. The design is an experiment in analog VGA signal generation, with documentation referencing a previous version for test modes. External hardware includes a VGA display, optional PMOD, and opamp circuits for current-to-voltage conversion.

The project titled 'Arko' has no meaningful documentation; the description and test instructions are placeholder text. The pin names are generic (in0-in7, io0-io7, out0-out7), suggesting a simple I/O or GPIO design, but the actual functionality is unknown. No external hardware or testing details are provided. The design cannot be evaluated due to insufficient information.

This design implements a transformer attention engine that computes a dot product over four terms from sequential 8-bit Q0.7 samples and outputs exp(mac/2) in UQ3.6 format. It uses a credit-based pipeline with handshake signals for input and output, processing four pairs of samples to produce a 9-bit result. The module is always ready for input and signals output validity, requiring acknowledgment from the master. It is intended for neural network or machine learning acceleration, though external hardware details are not specified.

Tiny Pong is a VGA display driver for a single-player Pong game, designed to output 640x480 video with 2-bit color per channel. It uses two buttons for paddle up and down control, and generates VGA HSYNC, VSYNC, and RGB signals. The chip is intended as a demo project for the Hacker Fab club at Case Western Reserve University, requiring a VGA monitor and a way to program the chip. The design is a fun and educational example of a simple game on an ASIC.
